documents: Banjan et al. (2023) Did the Younger Dryas to Holocene climate transition favour high seismicity rates in the north-western Alps? Sedimentology 70(2), 538-568; published version deposited as HAL hal-04032433 (PDF with HAL cover sheet)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (538-568); the HAL cover sheet is not counted

entry.evidence: However, the potential source of such an earthquake is unknown.

steps.action: The authors frame open problems in regional lacustrine palaeoseismology: the source of a large post-glacial MTD in Lake Bourget is unknown, and lake sensitivity changes with sedimentation rate across the Late Glacial to Holocene transition.
steps.quote: However, the potential source of such an earthquake is unknown.

steps.action: The authors acquired multibeam bathymetry of Lake Aiguebelette (2017) and 17.5 km of CHIRP seismic profiles (2020), and used existing La Thuile bathymetry; no seismic survey was run at La Thuile because the lake is shallow.
steps.quote: A total of 17.5 km of seismic profiles were acquired in November 2020 in Lake Aiguebelette by the iXblue company.

steps.action: The authors placed the coring sites in two subbasins far from the main tributaries to minimise flood deposits.
steps.quote: The coring sites were determined based on the bathymetric map in two different subbasins far from the main tributaries

steps.action: The authors retrieved cores AIG17III (about 16 m) and AIG17I (10.4 m) and extended THU10, then measured grain size, XRF core-scanning (log-ratios), LOI, ARM/IRM, AMS and P-wave velocity.
steps.quote: Relative variations in major elements were measured continuously every 5 mm by X-ray fluorescence (XRF)

steps.action: The authors built age-depth models from 14C AMS dates (IntCal20, R package clam, smooth spline) on event-free composite depths for AIG17III, AIG17I and THU10.
steps.quote: it was mandatory to first build an event-free composite depth for each sedimentary sequence before generating the age-depth model.

steps.action: The authors split the seismic data into Lower, Middle and Upper Units: the Middle Unit is transparent, about 1 m thick (converted with a Holocene P-wave velocity of 1410 m/s) and laterally continuous. Bathymetry shows a channel-shaped feature with levee bulges.
steps.quote: The Middle Unit is a transparent layer contrasting with the Upper Unit in terms of facies.

steps.action: The authors established the 115 cm event layer in AIG17III as a turbidite-homogenite distinct from background sediment: higher ln(Ca/Ti), a coarse graded base, about 4% AMS foliation in the homogenite, and lower ARM MDF.
steps.quote: All of these magnetic parameters indicate important differences in terms of magnetic mineralogy and magnetic grain sizes in each facies.

steps.action: The authors described the shallow-basin sequence AIG17I, which contains 21 event layers of 0.3 to 17.3 cm.
steps.quote: In the AIG17I sequence, twenty-one event layers are identified

steps.action: The authors dated the event layers after rejecting one inverted date per core: the AIG17III layer at 11 642-11 825 cal BP and the AIG17I 2 cm layer at 10 457-11 115 cal BP (extrapolated).
steps.quote: The large event layer in the deep basin sequence (AIG17III) has a depositional age that ranges between 11 642 and 11 825 cal BP

steps.action: In THU10 the authors identified a repeated sediment interval (623-723 cm matching 723-810 cm MCD) above a disturbed base, and interpreted it as an event layer.
steps.quote: the interval between 623 cm and 723 cm MCD appears to be a repetition of the interval between 723 cm and 810 cm MCD.

steps.action: The authors dated the THU10 event layer from a 14C sample 1 mm above it: 11 755 to 12 125 cal BP.
steps.quote: This sample has a depositional time range of 11 755 to 12 125 cal BP.

steps.action: The authors interpreted the homogenite and its high AMS foliation as a seiche deposit, and named two rival triggers: an earthquake or a large landslide.
steps.quote: Water mass oscillation in a lake may be induced by an earthquake (Campos et al., 2013) and/or a large proximal aerial or subaquatic landslide

steps.action: The authors correlated the seismic Middle Unit and the channelised MTD with the core event layer using thicknesses of the same order, the Ca/Ti source signature and the carbonate-free source area.
steps.quote: Then, the assumption that the channelized MTD and YD–EH event layers reflect the same object seems reasonable.

steps.action: The authors compared the deep and shallow basin event layers from independent cores and found them similarly aged, possibly from one triggering event; the shallow-basin chronology is less well constrained.
steps.quote: it is possible that the two similarly aged event layers were generated by the same triggering event.

steps.action: The authors interpreted the La Thuile event layer, 30 km away, as a translational slide and found its age similar to the Aiguebelette layers at the YD-EH transition.
steps.quote: This time range corresponds approximately to the Younger Dryas – Early Holocene transition, similarly aged in comparison with the event layers found in Lake Aiguebelette.

steps.action: The authors drew on published seismic profiles from Lakes Annecy and Bourget showing major MTDs between Late-Glacial and Holocene units.
steps.quote: Several major MTDs have been observed in other Alpine lakes in the YD–EH transition time range.

steps.action: The authors stated two rival hypotheses for the regional MTDs: climate-driven gravitational movements, or seismic energy released by stress changes after deglaciation.
steps.quote: Hence, two hypotheses will hereafter be discussed to explain the occurrence of similarly aged MTDs at the YD–EH transition

steps.action: The authors excluded near-field rockfalls as the common source: rockfall seismic waves attenuate, the 1248 CE Granier collapse left no significant MTD in these lakes, and no major rockfalls are known near the other lakes.
steps.quote: rockfalls as a source process to the event layer evidenced in the different sediment sequences presented here is very unlikely.

steps.action: The authors split the seismic hypothesis into Scenario 1 (one major regional earthquake) and Scenario 2 (moderate earthquakes near each lake).
steps.quote: Concerning the studied region, similarly aged events may be:

steps.action: The authors judged Scenario 1 most unlikely: there is no historical or palaeoseismic evidence of M>6.5, and the faults are short and segmented. A blind structure cannot be discarded.
steps.quote: Therefore, the authors consider Scenario 1 as being the most unlikely

steps.action: Under Scenario 2, the authors computed expected return periods of M5 to M6 earthquakes within 10 and 25 km of each lake from present-day Gutenberg-Richter rates (Drouet et al. 2020; Table 7).
steps.quote: roughly between 400 and 1300 years within a 25 km radius of each lake

steps.action: The authors compared these expected rates with the observed synchronous MTDs: under present-day rates, coeval MTDs are improbable, so YD-EH earthquake rates must have been higher.
steps.quote: This means that the probability of producing similarly aged significant MTDs in regional lakes is low.

steps.action: The authors set the result against published YD-EH MTDs and palaeoearthquakes in Swiss lakes, Achensee, Windermere, Vättern and Fennoscandia.
steps.quote: suggest similarly aged MTD events at ca 11 600 and ca 11 530 cal BP.

steps.action: The authors kept a seismic origin of the YD-EH event layers as the favoured explanation, supported by the seiche signature and regional synchroneity.
steps.quote: Among several possible explanations, a seismic origin is favoured, supported by sedimentological analysis

steps.action: The authors refined the claim: moderate nearby earthquakes at increased rates, possibly driven by deglaciation, mass transfer and stress rearrangement.
steps.quote: the authors propose that the evidenced event layers may be related to moderate nearby seismic events rather than from the occurrence of large regional events.

tree.answer: Yes: large MTDs and event layers at the YD-EH transition in several NW Alpine lakes
No; earthquakes are inferred from sediment traces
Explain the source of the coeval MTDs (cause)
Yes: climate-driven rockfall or gravitational failure versus seismicity; one regional large earthquake versus moderate local earthquakes
Partly: rockfall effects should stay local while seismicity explains regional synchroneity; the scenarios are separated by fault-length and recurrence arguments
Conditions found in past events known from traces

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes: repetition across lakes and basins (Aiguebelette deep and shallow, La Thuile, Annecy, Bourget)
Partly: replicated in an independent core and a second lake; age uncertainties are wide and no sensitivity tests were run
Seismic origin (moderate nearby earthquakes at higher rates) favoured as the best explanation

end.claim: The regionally synchronous YD-EH mass-transport deposits in NW Alpine lakes most likely record increased seismicity, probably moderate nearby earthquakes, linked to the climate transition and deglaciation, rather than rockfalls.

decisive_move.sentence: The radiocarbon age-depth models place the Aiguebelette and La Thuile event layers at the YD-EH transition; without this dating there is no regional synchroneity and no seismic argument.

gates.evidence: Cores and surveys were collected for general lake-record and palaeoseismic study; no hypothesis about YD-EH seismicity is stated as directing acquisition. Cores were taken in 2017, before the 2020 seismic survey (p. 544). The rockfall rival was set against attenuation and the Granier counter-example, and Scenario 1 against fault data (pp. 559-560), but the favoured seismic claim faced no test it could clearly fail. Nothing was fixed before the data: dates were rejected after calibration to avoid inversions (p. 551).

imports.item: Log-ratio transformation of compositional XRF data (Weltje et al. 2015)
R and the clam package for smooth-spline age-depth modelling
Laser particle-size analysers (Beckman Coulter, Malvern Mastersizer)
CHIRP sub-bottom profiler and multibeam echo-sounder
Superconducting magnetometer and high-resolution magnetic scanner (ARM/IRM)

novelty_claims.quote: In this paper, two new significant event layers will complete the list of existing MTDs identified in French peri-Alpine lakes
such a hypothesis has thus far never been tested.
At a regional scale a new MTD at the YD–EH transition in lake La Thuile, was also observed

limits: No review file or earlier version was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The paper reports no sensitivity tests of the age-depth models: spline parameters are given without justification and the rejection of two dates is justified only by avoiding inversions. The AIG17I event-layer age is extrapolated below the last dated sample. The THU10 age range in the Conclusion (11 652-12 426 cal BP) differs from the Results (11 755-12 125 cal BP); it looks like the calibrated range of the 6210 mm sample in Table 3 (inference). Table 7 and the text differ on the M>=6 regional rate (0.36 vs 0.38 events/year). The required ground-motion threshold (M5-6 within 25 km) is posited from a single 1822 case, not derived. The seiche signature does not by itself separate an earthquake from a landslide trigger. The link from climate transition to seismicity is supported by literature, not tested here. Sub-claims: depositional ages of the event layers, estimate_with_resolution (pp. 552, 555); the AIG17III event layer originates from the channelised MTD, best_explanation ('seems reasonable', p. 556); the rockfall rival is excluded as 'very unlikely' (p. 560); higher YD-EH earthquake rates are a conditional inference ('if this second hypothesis is valid', p. 561).

disagreements.target: Arnaud et al. (2012) maximum age of the Hautecombe Disturbed Unit in Lake Bourget
disagreements.support: The stratigraphic position of the HDU at the base of the Holocene drape (after Chapron et al.) places it nearer 11 700 cal BP.
disagreements.quote: In Arnaud et al. (2012), the maximum interpreted age of the HDU is 9900 cal BP.

disagreements.target: Large regional earthquake scenario (as proposed for Swiss lakes by Strasser et al. 2006) applied to the NW Alps
disagreements.support: There is no historical or palaeoseismic evidence of M>6.5 in the area, and regional faults are short and highly segmented; a blind structure is not excluded.
disagreements.quote: Therefore, the authors consider Scenario 1 as being the most unlikely

disagreements.target: Earthquake rates from current seismicity catalogues (Drouet et al. 2020) as representative of the YD-EH
disagreements.support: Return periods computed from present-day rates make coeval MTDs in several lakes improbable.
disagreements.quote: it implies that earthquake rates at the YD–EH transition might have been higher than those calculated from current earthquake catalogues.

disagreements.target: Vardy et al. (2010) slope-overloading explanation of YD-EH MTDs in Lake Windermere
disagreements.support: The authors cite Lowag et al. (2012), who found fluid escape structures pointing to increased seismic activity.
disagreements.quote: Vardy et al. (2010) postulated that the emplacement of these MTDs at the YD–EH transition may have solely been caused by slope overloading

alternatives_considered.chosen: Reject one 14C date per Aiguebelette core
alternatives_considered.reason: To avoid age inversions; possible contamination during sampling

alternatives_considered.chosen: No seismic survey in Lake La Thuile
alternatives_considered.reason: Shallow depth (8 m) causes near-simultaneous wave arrivals and multiples

alternatives_considered.chosen: Holocene P-wave velocity (1410 m/s) for time-depth conversion
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Velocity measured on Late Glacial facies
alternatives_considered.reason: No unopened cores of Late Glacial facies were available
To avoid the sediment matrix effect (Weltje et al. 2015)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Seismic origin of the coeval MTDs
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Climate-driven near-field rockfalls or gravitational movements
alternatives_considered.reason: Rockfall seismic waves attenuate with distance; the Granier collapse left no significant MTD; no major rockfalls near the other lakes

alternatives_considered.chosen: Scenario 2: moderate earthquakes near each lake
alternatives_considered.reason: No evidence of M>6.5; short, segmented faults
